description: A commit records a full snapshot of every tracked file at that moment, not a list of the lines that changed.

misconceptions.text: Many newcomers believe that a commit stores only the lines you changed.
A common mistake is to run git add notes.txt, keep typing in that file, and then assume the commit contains the later edits.

references: SRC-001, "The staging area sits in between"

section: How do I combine two branches?
description: Merging integrates one branch's own work into the branch you are standing on, either by moving a label forward or by recording a new commit with two parents.

misconceptions.text: A common mistake is to assume that merging must create a commit.
A common mistake is to think that deleting a branch deletes its work.

references: SRC-002, "How do I combine two branches?"
SRC-002, "Does merging delete the other branch?"

description: Resolving a merge conflict means editing the conflict markers Git leaves in a file, then staging and completing the merge; Git does not check by itself that the markers are gone before it accepts the commit.

misconceptions.text: A common mistake is to stage a file that still contains markers to clear the unmerged status.

A newcomer may believe any change both branches made to the same file will conflict, when only changes to the same or neighboring lines actually do; changes to lines that are not next to each other usually merge automatically.
